title: Concrete-Representational-Abstract (CRA)
preview: Start with real objects students can touch. Then move to pictures. Finally, use numbers and symbols. Builds understanding from the bottom up.

body.summary: Concrete-Representational-Abstract (CRA) means you teach math in three phases. CONCRETE: students touch actual objects (counters, blocks, coins). REPRESENTATIONAL: students draw pictures of those objects. ABSTRACT: students use numbers and symbols only. You move from phase to phase once the student is successful at the previous level. This is the single most-studied intervention approach for struggling math learners. You do not need fancy manipulatives — pennies, paper clips, or drawn dots all work.
body.whenToUse:
Use when a student gets the procedure wrong repeatedly, or when they can't explain WHY the math works. If they can do 3 × 4 but can't tell you what it means, CRA helps them build the understanding behind the numbers. Use for skills involving operations, fractions, ratios, or anything abstract.

Avoid using when the student already has a working mental model — don't undo what's working.
body.howToImplement:
1. GRAB CONCRETE OBJECTS. Anything countable works: pennies, paper clips, cubes, beans, even torn pieces of paper. You need a small pile.

2. CONCRETE PHASE (3-4 min): Rebuild the problem with objects.
   Example for "4 × 3":
   Say: "We're going to make 4 groups, and each group will have 3 things."
   Have the student physically make 4 piles of 3 pennies each.
   Ask: "How many pennies total?" Let them count.
   Say: "That's what 4 × 3 means — 4 groups of 3."

3. REPRESENTATIONAL PHASE (2-3 min): Move to pictures.
   Say: "Now let's draw what we just did. Draw 4 circles. Inside each circle, draw 3 dots."
   Let them count the dots. Connect: "This is the same as the pennies we just moved — we're just drawing them now."

4. ABSTRACT PHASE (2-3 min): Move to symbols.
   Say: "Now let's write it with numbers. 4 × 3. What does that equal?"
   If they say 12, say: "Yes — and that's the same 12 we got with pennies and with dots."

5. CHECK: Try one more problem at the abstract level. If they get it, great. If they don't, go back one phase.
body.teacherMoves:
IF the student resists touching objects ("that's baby stuff"):
→ Reframe: "These aren't kid toys — mathematicians use models all the time. Engineers build models. This is what smart people do."
→ Switch to paper-clip-sized objects that feel more grown-up (binder clips, coins).

IF the student rushes through concrete phase:
→ Slow them down: "Before we move to drawing, can you show me with the pennies one more time? I want to make sure I understand your thinking."

IF the student does concrete but can't move to abstract:
→ Spend MORE time in the representational (drawing) phase. Go back and forth between concrete and drawing several times before moving to numbers.

IF you don't have manipulatives:
→ Tear a piece of paper into 10-15 small squares. Use those as counters. Or use coins. Anything works.

IF the student already gets the abstract math:
→ Skip CRA. Only use it when the student is genuinely stuck on understanding.
body.variations:
TIER 2 (Standard CRA):
Use as described. Each phase is 2-3 minutes.

TIER 3 (Extended CRA):
Spend a whole session on Concrete before moving to drawings. Spend another session on drawings before moving to numbers. Don't rush the phases.

FRACTIONS VERSION:
Concrete: Use fraction tiles, paper strips, or pieces of a cookie to represent 1/2, 1/4, etc.
Representational: Draw bars and shade them.
Abstract: Write the fractions as numbers.

NEGATIVE NUMBERS VERSION:
Concrete: Use red chips (negative) and black chips (positive). Put them together and let zeros cancel.
Representational: Draw + and - signs in a box, cross out pairs.
Abstract: Write the equation.
body.researchBase: CRA is one of the most heavily researched intervention frameworks in mathematics (Miller & Mercer, 1993; Witzel, Mercer, & Miller, 2003). Meta-analyses show it produces large effect sizes for students with math learning disabilities (Jitendra et al., 2018). The National Center on Intensive Intervention recommends CRA as a core approach for Tier 2 and Tier 3 math intervention.
